b: CHICAGO — ‘Tis the season for holiday parties, end of year celebrations and making plans for the new year. These year-end activities are great for reflecting on the hard work that led to success in the past months and connecting with colleagues, but there is still professional etiquette to be aware of.

Be sure to keep yourself off the “naughty” list by maintaining professional standards at workplace functions, regardless of where they’re taking place at. To help, Trade Show Executive put together a short guide to make sure you stay on the “nice” list this year with helpful insights from HR professionals in the industry.
Do thank the people behind the party.

“Someone remembered the invitations, the dietary needs and the little details that helped everyone feel welcome,” said Hala Dean, Vice President, Organizational Learning & Development at Clarion Events. “Seek them out and offer a specific thank-you. ‘I noticed you made sure there was something I could eat. I really appreciated that,’ means more than a general ‘great party.’ Remember the people others may forget.”
Do help steer the conversation somewhere kinder.

“You don’t need to know someone’s personal history to interrupt a hurtful remark. A calm ‘We don’t know what people have experienced. Let’s leave that one alone,’ can change the direction without asking anyone to disclose anything,” Dean said. “If you made the remark, stop and apologize to the people who heard it. Take responsibility without explaining it away as ‘just a joke,’ or asking others to reassure you that it was fine.”

“The holiday party is not the time to discuss staffing shortages, payroll corrections, open positions or that one email nobody has responded to,” said Miguel Perez, Vice President of HR at United Service Companies. “Let’s give work a holiday, too!”

“Say hello to someone outside your department. It’s a great opportunity to meet coworkers you normally only know by their email signature,” Perez said. “And, make everyone feel welcome. The best holiday parties are the ones where everyone feels like part of the celebration.”
“You don’t need professional dance skills to have fun,” Perez said. “Just remember, nobody is handing out performance reviews based on your dance moves!”
Don’t make someone else’s enthusiasm the punchline.

“You don’t have to love the party theme to let other people enjoy it. I once heard an employee call a celebration ‘cringey’ and ‘childish’ to the person who had spent hours planning it. The organizer had been so excited, and you could see them deflate,” Dean said. “Sometimes acting unimpressed feels easier than showing enthusiasm, especially when we’re feeling unsure of ourselves. But people remember how we treat them. What do you want to be known for?”
Don’t turn the party into a staff meeting.
“No surprise performance reviews, no project updates and definitely no assigning new responsibilities between dinner and dessert,” Perez said.
Don’t overdo the holiday cheer or forget your professionalism at the door.

“If alcohol is available, enjoy responsibly. Remember, the goal is to celebrate the holidays, not become the most memorable topic of Monday’s morning meeting,” Perez said. ” A holiday party may be outside the office, but respect and appropriate behavior are always in season.”
Don’t assume you know everyone’s story.

“At a work gathering, I saw the mood change quickly when someone joked about a serious personal situation, then judged how another person should have handled it,” Dean said. “They knew nothing about the experiences of the people listening. Being colleagues doesn’t mean we know each other’s histories, and someone’s silence doesn’t mean they’re comfortable. Think before turning someone else’s circumstances into a joke or offering an easy answer to a complicated situation.”
Don’t be the DJ nobody hired.

“Song requests are welcome,” Perez said. “Taking over the music, announcing your own dance contest or requesting the same song five times might earn you a gentle visit from the holiday spirit committee.”
